--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Project Control Systems ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Describe** the monitoring-and-control loop and the performance measurement baseline. 2. **Read** the three earned-value curves: planned value (PV), earned value (EV), and actual cost (AC). 3. **Compute** schedule and cost variance and the SPI / CPI performance indices. 4. **Forecast** with EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI, and interpret them. 5. **Run** integrated change control so the baseline stays meaningful. 6. **Report** status honestly and recognize the "watermelon" trap.
Before we begin: the project has spent 60 % of its money --- is it 60 % done? Almost certainly not. "Percent of budget spent" and "percent of work finished" are different numbers, and the gap between them is the whole subject of this chapter.
## Introduction: from a plan to a control system You have planned the RC-vehicle project --- scope, WBS, schedule, budget. It is now **week 8**. The sponsor asks the only question that matters at this stage: **are we on track, and if not, how far off, and what will it cost to finish?** Answering that needs a **control system**: a closed loop that **measures** progress, **compares** it to the baseline, **analyzes** the variance, and drives a corrective **action** --- then measures again. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: The `label.size` argument of `geom_label()` is deprecated as of ggplot2 3.5.0. ℹ Please use the `linewidth` argument instead. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The monitoring-and-control loop. Without the 'compare to baseline' step, status reporting is just activity; with it, you get variance you can act on.](12-Project-Control-Systems_files/figure-epub/fig-control-loop-12-1.png){#fig-control-loop-12 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The reference for "compare" is the **performance measurement baseline** --- the approved **scope + schedule + cost** locked in at the end of planning ([Chapter 9](09-Cost-Estimation-and-Budgeting.qmd)'s S-curve is its cost dimension). ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** Earned value management is **contractually mandated** on large U.S. defense programs (EIA-748). Automotive programs run a lighter version at the milestone level. A food-plant capital project tracks committed vs. spent vs. installed. The math below is the same at every scale. :::
## The three curves Earned value management tracks three cumulative quantities against time: | Term | Also called | Meaning | |---|---|---| | **PV** --- Planned Value | BCWS | The budgeted cost of the work **scheduled** to be done by now | | **EV** --- Earned Value | BCWP | The budgeted cost of the work **actually done** by now | | **AC** --- Actual Cost | ACWP | What has actually been **spent** to do that work | **BAC** (Budget At Completion) is the total baseline budget --- where the PV curve ends. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The three curves through week 8 of the RC-vehicle project (BAC = $620 000, off the top of this view). By the status date EV sits below PV -- behind schedule -- and AC sits above EV -- over cost. The vertical gaps at week 8 are the schedule and cost variances.](12-Project-Control-Systems_files/figure-epub/fig-evm-curves-12-1.png){#fig-evm-curves-12 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## The six core metrics $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Schedule Variance} \quad SV &= EV - PV \\ \text{Cost Variance} \quad CV &= EV - AC \\ \text{Schedule Performance Index} \quad SPI &= EV / PV \\ \text{Cost Performance Index} \quad CPI &= EV / AC \end{aligned} $$ | Reading | Schedule | Cost | |---|---|---| | **Ahead / under** | $SV > 0$, $SPI > 1$ | $CV > 0$, $CPI > 1$ | | **On plan** | $SV = 0$, $SPI = 1$ | $CV = 0$, $CPI = 1$ | | **Behind / over** | $SV < 0$, $SPI < 1$ | $CV < 0$, $CPI < 1$ | ### Worked Example 1: the RC-vehicle project at week 8 Baseline budget **BAC = \$620 000**. By week 8 the plan said **35 %** of the work should be done; **30 %** is actually done; **\$210 000** has been spent. Live cell --- change the planned %, the actual %, or the actual cost. ```{webr-r} #| label: evm-example-12 BAC <- 620000 planned_pct <- 0.35 actual_pct <- 0.30 AC <- 210000 PV <- planned_pct * BAC EV <- actual_pct * BAC SV <- EV - PV CV <- EV - AC SPI <- EV / PV CPI <- EV / AC cat(sprintf("PV = $%s EV = $%s AC = $%s\n", format(PV, big.mark = " "), format(EV, big.mark = " "), format(AC, big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("SV = $%s (%s schedule)\n", format(SV, big.mark = " "), ifelse(SV < 0, "behind", "ahead"))) cat(sprintf("CV = $%s (%s budget)\n", format(CV, big.mark = " "), ifelse(CV < 0, "over", "under"))) cat(sprintf("SPI = %.3f (getting %.0f cents of schedule per planned dollar)\n", SPI, SPI * 100)) cat(sprintf("CPI = %.3f (getting %.0f cents of work per dollar spent)\n", CPI, CPI * 100)) ``` The project is **behind schedule and over cost** --- and this is visible in week 8, while there is still time to act, instead of as a surprise at the end. ## Forecasting | Forecast | Formula | Meaning | |---|---|---| | **EAC** (Estimate At Completion) | $BAC / CPI$ | Total cost if current cost efficiency holds | | EAC (schedule too) | $AC + \dfrac{BAC - EV}{CPI \times SPI}$ | If both cost *and* schedule performance persist | | EAC (one-off overrun) | $AC + (BAC - EV)$ | If the overrun so far was a one-time event | | **ETC** (Estimate To Complete) | $EAC - AC$ | Money still needed from here | | **VAC** (Variance At Completion) | $BAC - EAC$ | Projected total over/under budget | | **TCPI** (To-Complete Performance Index) | $\dfrac{BAC - EV}{BAC - AC}$ | The cost efficiency the *remaining* work must hit to still land on BAC | ### Try it yourself: EAC scenarios ```{webr-r} #| label: eac-scenarios-12 BAC <- 620000 EV <- 186000 AC <- 210000 PV <- 217000 CPI <- EV / AC SPI <- EV / PV eac_cpi <- BAC / CPI eac_oneoff <- AC + (BAC - EV) eac_cost_sched<- AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI * SPI) cat(sprintf("CPI = %.3f SPI = %.3f\n\n", CPI, SPI)) cat(sprintf("EAC, cost efficiency continues : $%s\n", format(round(eac_cpi), big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("EAC, overrun was a one-off : $%s\n", format(round(eac_oneoff), big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("EAC, cost AND schedule persist : $%s\n", format(round(eac_cost_sched), big.mark = " "))) etc <- eac_cpi - AC vac <- BAC - eac_cpi tcpi <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) cat(sprintf("\nETC (money still needed) : $%s\n", format(round(etc), big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("VAC (projected overrun) : $%s\n", format(round(vac), big.mark = " "))) cat(sprintf("TCPI (efficiency needed) : %.3f ", tcpi)) cat(ifelse(tcpi > 1.10, "-- that is a big ask; the BAC is likely unrealistic now.\n", ifelse(tcpi > 1.0, "-- recoverable, but the team must run leaner than planned.\n", "-- achievable.\n"))) ```
Which EAC formula should you actually report? It depends on *why* you are over. If a one-time event caused it (a failed test you have since fixed), $AC + (BAC - EV)$ is fair. If the overrun reflects how the team is fundamentally working (rates, productivity), $BAC/CPI$ is the honest number. If you are *also* behind schedule and recovery will cost overtime, the $CPI \times SPI$ version is the most conservative. Report the one your evidence supports --- and say which assumption you made.
## Reading the S-curve honestly - **Spend is not progress.** A project can be on budget (AC ≈ PV) and badly behind (EV ≪ PV) --- it just has not done the work yet. - **The "watermelon" report** --- green on the outside, red on the inside. High-level status shows green because spend matches plan, while the earned value underneath is red. - **Leading vs. lagging indicators.** SPI and CPI are somewhat lagging. Leading signals --- rising defect find-rate, slipping sub-milestones, key staff leaving --- warn you earlier. Watch both. ## Integrated change control Control only works against a **meaningful baseline**. Every change request goes through the same gate as in [Chapter 3](03-Scope-and-Organizational-Structures.qmd): assess the impact on scope, schedule, and cost; approve or reject; and if approved, **re-baseline** so future variance is measured against the new plan --- not the old one you can no longer hit. **Configuration management** keeps the product definition (drawings, specs, software versions) in step with the approved baseline. ## Status reporting The course's **Project Manager Report** and **Team Member Report** templates are the reporting instruments: they roll up progress, cost, schedule, risks, and issues on a fixed cadence. Good reporting is **honest** (report the red while it is still fixable), **consistent** (same metrics every period so trends are visible), and **actionable** (every variance has an owner and a next step). A dashboard that only ever shows green is not a control system --- it is a comfort blanket. ## Key Takeaways - **Control** is a closed loop: **measure → compare to baseline → analyze variance → act**, every reporting period. - Track **PV** (work scheduled), **EV** (work done), **AC** (money spent), all in budget dollars, against **BAC**. - $SV = EV - PV$, $CV = EV - AC$, $SPI = EV/PV$, $CPI = EV/AC$. Below 1 / negative = behind / over. - Forecast with **EAC** ($BAC/CPI$ is the common honest form), **ETC** $= EAC - AC$, **VAC** $= BAC - EAC$, **TCPI** $= (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC)$. - **Spend is not progress.** Beware the **watermelon** report; watch **leading** indicators, not just SPI/CPI. - Keep the **baseline meaningful** through integrated change control and configuration management. - Report **honestly, consistently, and actionably** --- every variance gets an owner. ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Full EVM snapshot BAC = \$400 000. At the status date: PV = \$180 000, EV = \$150 000, AC = \$165 000. Compute SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC (BAC/CPI), ETC, VAC, TCPI, and state the project's condition in one sentence. **Solution.** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BAC <- 400000; PV <- 180000; EV <- 150000; AC <- 165000 SV <- EV - PV; CV <- EV - AC; SPI <- EV / PV; CPI <- EV / AC EAC <- BAC / CPI; ETC <- EAC - AC; VAC <- BAC - EAC TCPI <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) cat(sprintf("SV=$%s CV=$%s SPI=%.3f CPI=%.3f\n", format(SV, big.mark=" "), format(CV, big.mark=" "), SPI, CPI)) cat(sprintf("EAC=$%s ETC=$%s VAC=$%s TCPI=%.3f\n", format(round(EAC), big.mark=" "), format(round(ETC), big.mark=" "), format(round(VAC), big.mark=" "), TCPI)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SV=$-30 000 CV=$-15 000 SPI=0.833 CPI=0.909 EAC=$440 000 ETC=$275 000 VAC=$-40 000 TCPI=1.064 ``` ::: ::: Behind schedule (SPI 0.83) and over cost (CPI 0.91); projected to finish about \$40 000 over budget, and the remaining work must run at TCPI ≈ 1.06 to still hit BAC.
Problem 2: On budget but in trouble A project reports PV = \$500 000, EV = \$400 000, AC = \$400 000. The sponsor sees "spend exactly matches earned value --- CPI = 1.0 --- we're fine." Are they? **Answer.** Cost efficiency is fine (CPI = 1.0), but **SPI = EV/PV = 0.80** --- the project has completed only 80 % of the work it should have by now. It is **20 % behind schedule** and will either finish late or need to spend more (overtime, added staff) to catch up, which will then push CPI below 1. This is the classic watermelon: the cost view is green, the schedule view is red.
Problem 3 (discussion): re-baseline or not? At week 8 the RC-vehicle project is forecast (EAC) at \$700 000 against a \$620 000 BAC, mostly because the retailer added a second body colourway (an approved scope change) and the new line's learning curve ran longer than planned. Should you re-baseline? **Discussion points.** Split the two causes. The **approved scope change** is a legitimate reason to re-baseline --- the extra colourway was authorised, so the budget and schedule should be formally updated and future variance measured against the new plan. The **learning-curve overrun** is *performance* against the plan, not a change to the plan --- that stays as variance you must recover or explain. Re-baselining to bury performance problems ("we'll just move the goalposts") destroys the value of the control system; re-baselining for authorised changes keeps it honest.
